agent_notes: The Hebrew verse is the superscription, which the KJV leaves unnumbered (39:0), so every later verse is one ahead of the KJV. The written form is Ketiv ידיתון (Radak: 'לידיתון, לידותון קרי'); I glossed the Qere and kept Jeduthun as a person, following Rashi and Meiri, with Metzudat Zion's 'instrument' reading noted.

STEPBible glosses נֶאֱלַמְתִּי as present 'I am dumb'; the form is a perfect, so I rendered it 'I have been struck dumb', which also repeats verse 3 and shows the echo. Radak and Metzudat David read it as a decision not to complain; Malbim as a stop to the question. I follow the first.

חֲמוּדוֹ is 'his desirable thing' (body, beauty, or wealth: Rashi flesh, Metzudat David riches, Ibn Ezra the body's desire). The KJV 'beauty' chooses one. 'Moth' (עָשׁ) is the clothes-moth larva, so the simile is cloth being eaten. I kept the Hebrew's openness.

תִּגְרָה in verse 11 is a hapax-like word. Rashi derives it from גרה 'to provoke' (Menahem), Ibn Ezra and Rashi's rival reading from גור 'fear'; Radak and Metzudat Zion link it to hitgarot 'to contend, make war' (Deut 2:5, 9). I took 'the contending of your hand' and listed it in the note on verse 11. The same two 'surely' words אַךְ וְהֶבֶל frame the whole psalm, so the repetition is deliberate.

Reviewer request addressed: 'no voice in court' and 'worked for hire' are removed. Ger is described as a resident outsider without land who depends on a host's protection; toshav as a settled alien (Radak, Metzudat Zion). The Lev 25:23 link is kept on the strength of Ibn Ezra's 'ככתוב בתורה'. The commentary mentions 1 Chr 29:15 because Radak cites it.

The five English versions split on the closing words: KJV/ASV/Webster keep 'stranger ... sojourner', BBE paraphrases to 'my time here is short'. I kept the two-term pair, since the Hebrew sets ger beside toshav on purpose.

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses הָשַׁע as 'smear' (H8159, from שׁעע/שׁעה II). I read it as the Hiphil imperative of שָׁעָה 'to gaze', so 'look away from me', which is how Rashi ('stay your hand from striking me'), Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion ('turn away', citing Isaiah 22:4 שעו מני) take it. The parallel Job 14:6 (שעה מעליו) has the same idiom; I cite it from my own knowledge, not from the packet.

אַבְלִיגָה is a cohortative of בָּלַג 'to brighten, show cheer'. The five English versions split: KJV/ASV/Webster 'recover strength', BBE 'be comforted', YLT 'brighten up'. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion gloss it 'be strong', but the cognate uses (Job 9:27, 10:20; Amos 5:9 in its causative sense) lean toward cheerfulness. I chose 'smile again' in the literal layer to keep both senses ('let me brighten').

agent_notes: בְּצֶלֶם is disputed: 'as a mere image/shadow' (most moderns, Ibn Ezra's second reading), 'in darkness' (Rashi, Donash, Radak, Meiri) and 'in the image [of God]' (Targum, Malbim). I chose 'in a shadow-image' for the literal layer, which keeps the ambiguity between 'image' and 'shade'. The literal also keeps the plural verb יֶהֱמָיוּן, which agrees with the collective 'a person'.
